newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lazard head denies succession crisis at bank.
newsitem.headline: Lazard head denies succession crisis at bank.

text.p: The chairman of Lazard Freres, Michel David-Weill, denied reports on Wednesday there was any succession crisis at the prestigious corporate finance house or that he had ever annointed his son-in-law to take over from him.

Breaking his silence after persistent media reports of a power struggle at the tripod investment bank which has operations in Paris, New York and London, David-Weill, 64, said in French newspaper interviews he was in no hurry to retire.

Contrary to widespread suggestions, he added he had never groomed his son-in-law Edouard Stern, 42, to take over from him at the 150-year-old family-run merchant bank. "There never was a successor," he told business daily Les Echos.

Talk that Stern, who is married to David-Weill's eldest daughter, was being prepared to take the reins at the traditionally secretive investment firm has been rife ever since he joined the company in 1992.
David-Weill's family have been dominant players in the transatlantic banking firm for four generations, but none of his four daughters has shown a strong interest in banking.
Referring to his retirement, David-Weill said, "I still have time". Under the bank's statutes, he can remain at the helm for another eight years.
He said he envisaged a change in management style at the investment house, although not immediately.
"We need to prepare on a horizon of 10 to 15 years for a more collegiate management style like some American banks have," he told Le Figaro.
The three Lazard houses, grouped under Lazard Partners, work mainly in corporate advisory services, including mergers and acquisitions, asset management and trading activities.

Stern, contacted last week, said there was "no foundation" to a Le Monde report that he had fallen out with David-Weill or that he had aroused antagonism in fellow partners because of what the newspaper described as his abrupt manner.

David-Weill said it "would have been crazy...for him (Stern) to take on the role of heir-apparent. That's a role that's good for two years, because when it (the succession) doesn't take place right away, the successor is cooked."
David-Weill said Stern was an important partner and "I think he will be a great banker." Asked whether Stern would be with the group in another year, he replied yes.

He said he had no worries about U.S. investment banks' growing muscle in the French market. French newsletter Capital Finance reported this week U.S.-based Goldman Sachs edged out Lazard Freres in mergers activity last year in France.
"Competition is healthy," he said, at the same noting that despite a more aggressive performance by its rivals, Lazard had enjoyed record profits in 1996.
